title: Fat Bear Week Returns for Its 12th Year
summary:
Every fall, millions of people tune in to watch brown bears get ready for winter. Then they vote for the fattest one. It's called Fat Bear Week, and it's now in its 12th year.

The contest takes place at Katmai National Park in Alaska, a 4.1-million-acre wilderness of volcanoes, rivers, and forests. About 2,200 brown bears live there, feasting on salmon-rich rivers. There are no roads into the park — visitors arrive by boat or plane.

Fat Bear Week began in 2014, when park ranger Mike Fitz noticed two photos of the same bear on the park's website. One was taken in June, the other in September. The bear had gained a huge amount of weight. Bears rely on those fat reserves to survive the long winter. Fitz and other rangers turned the idea into a one-day Facebook event called "Fat Bear Tuesday," where votes were counted through "likes." The next year, it expanded into a full week and drew hundreds of thousands of participants.

How does it work? It's a single-elimination competition. Each day, fans vote online for one of two bears in a head-to-head matchup. The bear with the most votes advances; the other is eliminated. The rounds continue until two bears remain. The final vote is on September 29, 2026.

This year, 16 bears and bear families are competing. Bear 32, or Chunk, is back to defend his 2025 title after recovering from a broken jaw. He faces Bear 164, known as Bucky, who wowed fans by snatching leaping salmon out of the air. Bear 132 is competing while raising three cubs — one of whom survived alone for several days this summer before reuniting with the family. Bear 806 is raising her own cub plus an adopted young bear named Biggie.

In 2025, more than 1.7 million votes were cast from over 100 countries. Whether you vote for the returning champion or a newcomer, Fat Bear Week is a fun way to follow these amazing animals — and a reminder of the importance of protecting their wild Alaskan home.
why_it_matters: Fat Bear Week shows how a cheap, funny idea can turn a remote national park into a global classroom, turning casual viewers into people who know something about salmon runs, winter fat reserves and the wild places most of them will never visit.

background_read: Katmai National Park sits on the Alaska Peninsula (a long stretch of land reaching toward the Aleutian Islands), and there are no roads into it — people arrive by boat or small plane, which is part of why its bears live so undisturbed.
Each summer and fall, sockeye salmon swim up the park's rivers to spawn, and bears crowd places like Brooks Falls to catch them — some snatch leaping fish straight out of the air.

Brown bears are the same species as grizzly bears; coastal Alaskan brown bears grow much larger thanks to all that salmon, and they need the fat to get through winter, when they stay in dens and can lose a large share of their body weight.

Mike Fitz (the Katmai ranger who came up with the contest and later became a resident naturalist for the park's live bear cameras) turned two photos into an event that fans now compare to March Madness (the U.S. college basketball tournament built on single-elimination brackets).

Katmai is also famous for the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes, the scar left by a huge volcanic eruption in the early 1900s — one of the largest of the twentieth century — a reminder that this wilderness is shaped by forces far bigger than its bears.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — global attention for a small park
perspectives.description: A contest that costs almost nothing turns Katmai into a yearly worldwide event watched in more than 100 countries. The live cameras let people follow individual bears, their cubs and their recoveries, which builds real emotional attachment to a place with no roads.

Voting on how fat an animal is can turn wild bears into internet characters. Critics point out the contest says nothing about the pressures that actually decide whether bears eat well — shrinking salmon runs, warming rivers and development near protected land.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — a biology lesson in disguise
perspectives.description: Underneath the bracket is a simple energy equation: eat enough salmon in fall, store the fat, and survive to spring. Wrapping that science in a public vote is an efficient way to make a biological fact memorable and easy to track year after year.

The real test is what happens after the final vote. If those millions of voters also back salmon habitat protection or follow the park's research, the contest becomes more than entertainment; if they click away until next fall, the bears are just a seasonal meme.
